accepted.question_text: Let S be a semi-algebraic subset of R^k defined by s polynomial equalities and inequalities whose degrees are bounded by d. Is there an algorithm that computes all Betti numbers of S in time single exponential in k? More concretely, can the currently known single-exponential methods for computing only the first l Betti numbers for fixed l be extended to compute the full Betti sequence of S within a single-exponential running time in the ambient dimension?
accepted.context_brief: Single-exponential algorithms for all Betti numbers

evidence.quote: Computing Betti Numbers in Single Exponential Time ? Suppose S subset R^k is a semi-algebraic set defined in terms of s polynomials, of degrees bounded by d. One of the most fundamental open questions in algorithmic semi-algebraic geometry, is whether there exists a single exponential (in k) time algorithm for computing the Betti numbers of S.

The best we can do so far is summarized in Theorem 6.10 which gives the existence of single exponential time algorithms for computing the first l Betti numbers of S for any constant l. A big challenge is to extend these ideas to design an algorithm for computing all the Betti numbers of S.

accepted.question_text: For semi-algebraic sets, are the middle Betti numbers intrinsically harder to compute than the lowest and highest Betti numbers or the Euler-Poincare characteristic? In particular, is there a complexity-theoretic hardness result that explains the apparent algorithmic gap, or an analogue of the phenomenon from smooth projective complex varieties in which the middle Betti numbers contain essentially all the information?

evidence.quote: Are the Middle Betti Numbers Harder to Compute ? From the algorithm design perspective it seems that computing the lowest (as well as the highest) Betti numbers of semi-algebraic sets, as well the Euler-Poincare characteristic of semi-algebraic sets, are easier than computing the "middle" Betti numbers.

Is there a complexity-theoretic hardness result that would justify this fact? In certain mathematical contexts (for instance, the topology of smooth projective complex varieties) the middle Betti numbers contain all the information. Is there a complexity-theoretic analogue of this phenomenon that would justify our experience that certain Betti numbers are harder to compute than the others?

accepted.question_text: Consider a semi-algebraic set in R^k defined by l quadratic inequalities. Can the number of connected components of such a set be computed by an algorithm with complexity k^O(l), or even k^O(l^2), rather than the currently best known k^(2^O(l)) type bound coming from the available all-Betti-number methods? Equivalently, is there a substantially more efficient algorithm for counting connected components in the quadratic case than the general-purpose approach currently provides?

evidence.quote: More Efficient Algorithms for Computing the Number of Connected Components in the Quadratic Case ? For semi-algebraic sets in R^k defined by l quadratic inequalities, there are algorithms for deciding emptiness, as well as computing sample points in every connected component whose complexity is bounded by k^O(l) [3, 45]. We also have an algorithm [9] for computing the Euler-Poincare characteristic of such sets whose complexity is k^O(l).

However, the best known algorithm for computing the number of connected components of such sets has complexity k^(2^O(l)) (as a special case of the algorithm for computing all the Betti numbers given in Theorem 2.6). This raises the question whether there exists a more efficient algorithm with complexity k^O(l) or even k^O(l^2) for counting the number of connected components of such sets.

accepted.question_text: For a general semi-algebraic set, can the exponent O(k^2) in the complexity of roadmap algorithms be improved to O(k), so that testing connectivity has asymptotically the same complexity as testing emptiness? More broadly, can one design roadmap or connecting-path algorithms whose complexity improvement would also yield sharper effective bounds on the lengths of semi-algebraic connecting paths?
accepted.context_brief: Improve roadmap complexity for general sets

evidence.quote: More Efficient Algorithms for Computing the Number of Connected Components for General Semi-algebraic Sets ? A very interesting open question is whether the exponent O(k^2) in the complexity of roadmap algorithms (cf. Theorem 4.15) can be improved to O(k), so that the complexity of testing connectivity becomes asymptotically the same as that of testing emptiness of a semi-algebraic set (cf. Theorem 4.12).
An improvement in the complexity of algorithms for constructing connecting paths (such as the roadmap algorithm) would also improve the bound on the length of connecting paths.
